sudoku.title: Sudoku solver
sudoku.description:
Sudoku is a logic-based, combinatorial number-placement puzzle. The objective is to fill a 9×9 grid with digits so that each column, each row, and each of the nine 3×3 sub grids that compose the grid contains all of the digits from 1 to 9. The puzzle setter provides a partially completed grid, which for a well-posed puzzle has a single solution.

I was solving puzzles while traveling, when I thought to myself "I wonder how hard it would be to solve these puzzles programmatically" and this resolver tool is the answer to that question.

instructions.title: Instructions
instructions.0: Click a cell to change its value by typing a number
instructions.1: Fill the field according to the puzzle you want to solve
instructions.2: Cells that are colored red, are in conflict with each other
instructions.4: Press "Clear" to set all cells back to empty
instructions.5: Use any of the example buttons for a prefilled field

kana.title: Kana learning tool
kana.description:
Before I went to Japan for an internship, I wanted to at least be able to read the basic character sets, called "Hiragana" and "Katakana" respectively.
Of course, having a developer mindset, I had to make a tool that does exactly what I would like it do.

instructions.title: Instructions
instructions.0:
The concept of this tool is that by repeating a selected sets of characters, that after repeating it enough they will be stored in the long term memory.
The following options are available;
instructions.1: repeat: the number of times to repeat each set in a single session
instructions.2: font: some fonts make the characters look slightly different
instructions.3: reverse mode: this will switch the tool from "kana to latin" to "latin to kana"
instructions.4: Select the characters by clicking the checkbox to their right, after which you can press the button to start.

concepts.title: Programming Concepts
concepts.description: Here are a few examples of concepts and challenges that I had to confront while working as a developer. I will break down my approach and show example of what I did to overcome these challenges.

password.title: What is a Safe Password?
password.description: With an increasing amount of data leaks, and password policies trying to get users to use "secure" passwords. What really is the best approach of creating a password?
password.story:
The problem

We all have been in this situation, "your password most contain at least one capital, a number, etc...". But does this really make your password more secure? Or does it just make your password harder to remember?
Of course, the best solution is to have a password manager, but these are not completely foolproof either. A unique password with either a second or maybe even a third authentication step would be the most secure.

A good example that happened to me, for an application we needed the users to register a 6 digit PIN code. However, somebody in a different team designed a policy for such PIN codes, the policy was something similar to this: "No dates (YYYYMM, MMYYYY, MMDDYY, DDMMYY, etc.), No sequential numbers, No keyboard patterns, No username (we used number based users)" and some more requirements.
The end result? More than 60% of the numbers between 000000-999999 were not allowed.
So in the end not only was this a potential big nuisance to the users, as any "logical" PIN would be denied, it also made brute-forcing the PIN codes a lot easier because only 40% of the 6 digit PIN codes were left.

Conclusion

Beside educating users on what a good password or PIN is, we also need to be aware that creating difficult requirements might end up causing the opposite effect. Because when something is hard to remember, people might employ tricks to "remember" their password (e.g. putting it a post-it)
Therefore, fewer requirements might actually increase the security of a password or PIN

search.title: Story of a Full-Text Product Search
search.description: Relational database are often the cornerstone of efficient data storage. They are tried and tested for handling structured data with complex relations. But what if we need to venture beyond their strengths? Specifically, what if we need to perform full-text search across data, provide a list of options to filter through, and return all information as a cohesive document?
story: Relation databases are often not optimized for large, full-text queries. Moreover, retrieving deeply nested relationships can severely impact performance, especially when the data size grows. Let's consider the following example;
Enter Elasticsearch: Full-Text Search and Scalability

To overcome these challenges, we turned to Elasticsearch. By indexing the data as documents that closely resemble the desired JSON structure, we simplified both retrieval and search. Elasticsearch excels at full-text search and offers a host of optimization opportunities.
As example, we implemented a routing based on the "storeId" field, ensuring that all queries for a specific store are always directed to the same instance. This significantly reduces query latency and boosts cluster efficiency
The results speak for themselves. We built a product search system capable of handling over 10GB of data across 1,000+ stores. Even with such scale, search queries consistently delivered results in less than 100ms (end-to-end).

bots.title: Battling Bot Traffic
bots.description: During a routine network analysis, we noticed an unusual pattern: one of our public search endpoints was experiencing a massive influx of traffic. The culprit? Bots.
story:
Blocking them seemed like the obvious solution at first, but it quickly turned into a game of whack-a-mole. Each time we blocked a group of bots, they returned using a different approach, mimicking legitimate users up to the point that we were unable to see the difference aside from the high load created. It was clear that endlessly trying to block these bots would not be sustainable, but neither was leaving the API as it was, as at this point bots almost account for 90% of the load, straining our resource and driving up costs.
The situation was further complicated by the fact that we couldn't block the API entirely either. Not only were legitimate users relying on it, but so did our homepage. The question became: how do we significantly reduce bot traffic without impacting our users?
Rethinking the approach: making the environment unattractive

Initially, we tried conventional solutions like blocking suspicious traffic or employing WAF rules to filter out bots. While effective to some extent, these measures just weren't enough. Bots kept evolving, adapting their strategies to bypass our defenses.
So, we were forced to shift our mindset. Instead of trying to eliminate bots entirely, we asked ourselves: What if we make the environment less attractive to them?
The answer lays in hitting them where it hurts: their running costs.

Unintentionally, we created the perfect environment for bots. The API provided high value data, and delivered it at blazing speed.
We considered slowing down the API, but this would only create another problem: bots would simply spread their request across a wider range of IPS, increasing their network footprint. Worse, in the end this would cost us even more while also reducing the speed for legitimate users. Instead, we needed a method that could slow down bots, that rather would add to our costs, would costs them instead.
The solution? Cryptographic challenges.

Here is an example of how it works;

Every API request is accompanied by a challenge. To access the API, the client must solve this challenge by finding the value that, when salted with the "nonce" (a unique, random value), produces the hash in the "challenge".
The challenge is simple in concept, but computationally expensive to solve. For example, in the case above, solving the challenge might in the worst case require up to 16.7 million possible combinations (256<sup>3</sup>). While modern hashing algorithms like SHA-512 are fast, running them millions of times takes significant time and resources.
However, once the correct answer is found, in this case "608ec2", it is trivial to verify and requires almost no resources on our server. Furthermore, it is relatively easy to tune the challenge, by lowering the amount of digits needed to reach an answer. (or rather, the amount of bits)

This solution proved highly effective. Legitimate users were largely unaffected thanks to the capability of be able to dynamically tune the challenge, while bots struggled to keep up with the increased computational demands. By raising the cost of operation for bots, we reduced their traffic dramatically, easing the load on our API and cutting expenses.

This experience taught us an important lesson: sometimes the best defense isn't offense, but rather saddling your adversary with costs that make their efforts costlier than the value they gain.

sudoku.title: Sudoku solver
sudoku.description:
Een sudoku is een puzzel bestaande uit negen bij negen vakjes die gegroepeerd zijn als negen blokken van drie bij drie vakjes. In de vakjes moeten de cijfers 1 tot en met 9 ingevuld worden op zo'n manier dat in elke horizontale lijn en in elke verticale kolom en in elk van de negen blokjes de cijfers 1 tot en met 9 één keer voorkomen. In een aantal vakjes zijn de cijfers al ingevuld.

Tijdens een vliegreis was ik sudoku's aan het oplossen, toen ik mezelf aanvroeg "Hoe lastig kan het zijn om een sudoku programmatisch optelossen" en deze tool is het antwoord daar op.

instructions.title: Instructies
instructions.0: Klik in een cel, en typ een number om de waarde aan te passen
instructions.1: Vul het veld in referentie naar de sudoku die u wilt oplossen
instructions.2: Cellen die rood gekleurd zijn, zijn in conflict met elkaar
instructions.3: Druk op "Los op" om de puzzel automatisch optelossen
instructions.4: Druk op "Wissen" om het veld te legen
instructions.5: Gebruik een van de "voorbeeld" knoppen voor een vooraf ingevulde sudoku

sudoku.title: Sudoku solver
sudoku.description:
Sudoku ist eine Gattung von Logikrätseln, die aus den lateinischen Quadraten entstand. In der üblichen Version ist es das Ziel, ein 9×9-Gitter mit den Ziffern 1 bis 9 so zu füllen, dass jede Ziffer in jeder Einheit genau einmal vorkommt, und in jedem der 81 Felder exakt eine Ziffer vorkommt.

Während einer Flugreise löste ich Sudoku-Rätsel und fragte mich dabei: „Wie schwer kann es sein, ein Sudoku programmgesteuert zu lösen?“ Und dieses Tool ist die Antwort darauf.

instructions.title: Anleitung
instructions.0: Klicken Sie in eine Zelle und geben Sie eine Zahl ein, um den Wert anzupassen
instructions.1: Füllen Sie das Feld für das Sudoku aus, das Sie lösen möchten
instructions.3: Drücken Sie "Lösen", um das Sudoku automatisch zu lösen
instructions.4: Drücken Sie "Leeren", um das Feld zu leeren
instructions.5: Verwenden Sie eines der Beispiele für ein vorausgefülltes Sudoku

kana.title: Kana learning tool
kana.description:
Vorher ich für ein Praktikum nach Japan ging, wollte ich zumindest die einfachsten Alphabete lernen, welchen „Hiragana“ und „Katakana“ heißen.
Und da ich eine Entwickler Mentalität habe, war der nächste logische Schritt natürlich, selber ein Tool zu erstellen.

instructions.title: Anleitung
instructions.0:
Die Idee hinter diesem Tool besteht darin, dass eine Reihe von Zeichen bei häufiger Wiederholung im Langzeitgedächtnis gespeichert wird.
Die nächsten Einstellungen sind verfügbar:
instructions.1: wiederholen: wie oft alles in einer einzigen Sitzung wiederholt werden soll
instructions.2: font: Einige "Fonts" lassen die Zeichen etwas anders aussehen
instructions.3: reverse mode: Dieser Modus kehrt die Übersetzungsreihenfolge um.
instructions.4: Wählen Sie die Zeichen aus, indem Sie auf die Checkbox rechts klicken. Anschließend können Sie auf „Start“ klicken.
